title: Schur Number Five (S(5) = 160) Settled After 101 Years via Formally Certified 2-Petabyte SAT Proof
aiSystem: Cube-and-Conquer SAT Solver (Massively Parallel SAT + Certified DRAT Checker)
whyItMatters: Marijn Heule settled Issai Schur’s 101-year-old Ramsey-theory problem (1916), proving S(5) = 160 via massively parallel SAT solving and certifying a record 2-petabyte proof with a formally verified checker.
summary: Posted on November 21, 2017 (and published at AAAI-18), Marijn J. H. Heule at the University of Texas at Austin resolved the century-old Schur Number Five problem posed by Issai Schur in 1916: finding the largest integer n such that {1, …, n} can be 5-colored without a monochromatic solution to a + b = c. Encoding the problem into propositional logic and applying massively parallel Cube-and-Conquer SAT solving on the Stampede supercomputer, Heule proved S(5) = 160 and validated the resulting 2-petabyte unsatisfiability proof—ten times larger than the 2016 Pythagorean Triples proof—using a formally verified proof checker.
technicalHighlights: Settled Issai Schur’s 1916 Ramsey-theory problem after 101 years, proving S(5) = 160.
Constructed and mechanically certified a 2-petabyte clausal proof—demonstrating formal verification scales to petabyte-class automated reasoning.
Advanced Cube-and-Conquer partitioning heuristics subsequently used to resolve Keller’s Conjecture in dimension 7.
caveats: The 2-petabyte proof is purely machine-verifiable rather than human-readable, offering no short conceptual explanation for why 160 is the exact threshold.

scoreRationale.foundational: Resolved a classical 101-year-old problem in Ramsey theory and additive combinatorics.
scoreRationale.ripple: Proved that formally verified SAT proof checkers can scale to petabyte-level automated mathematical proofs.
scoreRationale.verification: Certified end-to-end by a formally verified clausal proof checker and peer-reviewed at AAAI-18.
scoreRationale.velocity: Cracked a combinatorial coloring threshold that resisted a century of mathematical and computational attacks.
